About: Collisions in 1D

Source

Model
Masses 0.1–3 kg, velocities −3…3 m/s, elasticity 0–100%, track x ∈ [−2, 2] m, ball radius (3m/4πρ)^⅓ with ρ = 35 kg/m³ (or 0.15 m constant), standard restitution formulas — including walls reflecting with v → −e·v.
Concept
Conservation of momentum: Σp = Σmᵢvᵢ is unchanged by every ball–ball collision, whatever the masses or elasticity. Kinetic energy is conserved only when e = 100%.
Serves
The two conservation laws side by side: watch Σp stay fixed through elastic, partial and perfectly inelastic collisions while KE drops by exactly the amount the collision dissipates.
Inquiry
What survives a crash? Predict outcomes for equal masses, sticking collisions, and unequal masses — then read Σp and KE off the live ledger.
Misconception
That inelastic collisions destroy momentum. They cannot: only kinetic energy degrades (to deformation and heat); Σp survives every collision. Momentum only changes when an external push acts — the reflecting walls demonstrate exactly that.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict: the classic head-on

Two identical balls (0.5 kg each). Ball 1 rolls at +1 m/s toward ball 2, which is at rest. The collision is perfectly elastic (e = 100%). What happens when they meet?

2 · Read the ledger

Watch the bottom badges (or open Readouts): before the collision Σp = +0.50 kg·m/s and KE = 0.25 J — and after it, exactly the same. The motion moved from one ball to the other, but the totals never flinched. That is what "conserved" means.

3 · Predict: a sticky crash

Elasticity is now 0% — perfectly inelastic. Ball 1 (0.5 kg, +1 m/s) hits a heavy ball 2 (1.5 kg, at rest) and they will stick together. What survives the crash?

4 · Dial the elasticity

Now e = 50%. Watch a collision, then sweep the Elasticity slider and replay by dragging the balls back. At every setting Σp is identical before and after the collision — while KE drops on impact: not at all at 100%, the most at 0%. Elasticity decides only how much kinetic energy the crash burns, never the momentum.

5 · The universal law

Unequal masses now — 0.5 kg meets 1.5 kg with the reflecting border on. Light bounces back, heavy plods on, yet Σp = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ is unchanged through every ball–ball collision. Watch the wall bounces though: Σp flips there, because the wall pushes from outside the system — exactly why the law says isolated system. Hit Finish and explore freely.

The Physics

Collisions in 1D · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Balls on a short track run into each other, or into the walls, while two running totals, the momentum Σp and the kinetic energy KE, are tallied on screen. It shows what a collision does to each total and how the elasticity e changes the result.

What you'll learn

  • How the total momentum Σp and the kinetic energy KE compare before and after a collision.
  • What the elasticity e controls, and how the masses decide who moves off how fast.
  • How a wall differs from a second ball.
The track from −2 m to +2 m with a wall at each end, two balls moving toward each other, and the two badges at the bottom.

What's on screen

  • Balls: numbered and coloured, with the mass under each. A heavier ball is drawn larger. Up to four balls can share the track.
  • Velocity arrow above each ball, pointing the way it moves. Right is positive.
  • Walls at ±2 m, and a ruler below the track in metres.
  • Badges at the bottom: the elapsed time t on the left, and Σp and KE on the right.
See itPress Play and watch the two balls approach each other. Watch for: the arrows showing ball 1 moving right and ball 2 moving left, and the Σp and KE badge at the bottom right.

03

Total momentum is conserved in every ball-to-ball collision

Velocity is positive to the right. For two balls, the total momentum Σp = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ is the same just after a collision as just before it:

m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′
Momentum before = momentum after (a prime marks the velocity after the collision).

While the balls touch, each pushes on the other with a force of the same size in the opposite direction, for the same time. One ball gains exactly the momentum the other loses. This needs the two balls to be on their own, with nothing outside pushing them, and it holds for any masses and any elasticity.

At the opening setup, Σp = 0.5 × (+1) + 1.5 × (−0.5) = −0.25 kg·m/s. At e = 100% the balls leave at −1.25 m/s and +0.25 m/s, and Σp = 0.5 × (−1.25) + 1.5 × 0.25 = −0.25 kg·m/s again.

See itPress Play and watch the Σp badge through the collision. Watch for: each ball's p changing at the collision while the Σp badge stays at −0.25 kg·m/s.
04

Elasticity sets how much of the closing speed comes back

The elasticity e compares how fast the balls separate with how fast they approached:

e = −(v₁′ − v₂′) / (v₁ − v₂)
Speed of separation ÷ speed of approach, between 0 and 1.

e = 1 (100% on the slider) is a perfectly elastic collision and e = 0 is perfectly inelastic, where the balls move on together. Momentum conservation and this definition together fix both final velocities. The kinetic energy lost is ½ [m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)] (1 − e²)(v₁ − v₂)², so KE is conserved only when e = 1.

Take ball 1 (0.5 kg, +1 m/s) hitting ball 2 (1.5 kg, at rest) with e = 0.5. The balls leave at −0.125 m/s and +0.375 m/s, so the separation speed is 0.5 = 0.5 × 1. Σp stays at +0.50 kg·m/s while KE falls from 0.25 J to 0.109 J.

See itPress Play and watch both badges at the collision. Watch for: the Σp badge staying at +0.50 kg·m/s while the KE badge drops from 0.25 J to 0.11 J.
05

Sticking together loses the most kinetic energy

At e = 0 the balls leave the collision with the same velocity, found from momentum alone:

v′ = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂) / (m₁ + m₂)
The pair carries the whole Σp, so v′ = Σp ÷ total mass.

This is the velocity of the centre of mass, which is the same before and after the collision. With ball 1 (0.5 kg, +1 m/s) and ball 2 (1.5 kg, at rest), v′ = 0.5 ÷ 2.0 = +0.25 m/s. KE falls from 0.25 J to ½ × 2.0 × 0.25² = 0.0625 J, so three quarters is lost. No other e loses more, because the loss is largest at e = 0.

The lost energy is not destroyed. It becomes deformation, heat and sound, which the sim does not draw.

See itPress Play and follow the × marker of the centre of mass. Watch for: the pair moving off together at +0.25 m/s, the KE badge dropping to 0.06 J, and the × moving steadily the whole time.
06

Equal masses swap velocities in an elastic collision

At e = 1 both Σp and KE are conserved, and that fixes the outcome. If the masses are equal, the balls simply exchange velocities: v₁′ = v₂ and v₂′ = v₁. A moving ball hitting an equal ball at rest stops dead and the target leaves with its speed.

With unequal masses and a target at rest, v₁′ = [(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)] v₁ and v₂′ = [2m₁/(m₁ + m₂)] v₁. A light ball bounces back from a heavy one, which moves off slowly. A heavy ball keeps going and sends the light one ahead of it.

ball 1 → ball 2 at rest, v₁ = +1 m/sball 1 afterball 2 after
0.5 kg → 0.5 kg0 m/s+1.0 m/s
0.5 kg → 1.5 kg−0.5 m/s+0.5 m/s
1.5 kg → 0.5 kg+0.5 m/s+1.5 m/s
See itPress Play and watch the collision of two equal balls. Watch for: ball 1 stopping dead and ball 2 leaving at +1.00 m/s, with Σp and KE both unchanged.
See itNow watch a light ball meet a heavy one. Watch for: the light ball 1 bouncing back at −0.50 m/s while ball 2 moves off at +0.50 m/s.
07

A wall changes Σp because it pushes from outside

With Reflecting border on, a ball that reaches a wall at ±2 m reverses its velocity and keeps the fraction e of its speed: v → −e·v. At e = 100% it comes back at the same speed.

A single 0.5 kg ball moving at +1 m/s has Σp = +0.50 kg·m/s. After it bounces off the right wall it moves at −1 m/s, so Σp = −0.50 kg·m/s. The wall belongs to no ball, so its push is a force from outside, and the conservation of Σp for the balls no longer applies. The 1.00 kg·m/s that Σp changed by goes to the wall and whatever holds it.

At a lower e the ball returns slower. The bounce still reverses Σp, and KE falls by the factor e².

See itPress Play and wait for the ball to reach the right wall, about 2.9 s after the start. Watch for: the Σp badge flipping from +0.50 to −0.50 kg·m/s at the bounce, and the momentum arrow under the ball reversing.
08

Where it matters

  • Car crashes. A crash is close to perfectly inelastic. The momentum of the two cars together is the same just after impact as just before, and the lost kinetic energy goes into bending metal. Crumple zones make that happen over a longer time.
  • The ballistic pendulum. A bullet stuck in a block is an e = 0 collision, so mv = (m + M)v′. The swing that follows is then used with energy to find v′, and from it the bullet's speed.
  • Newton's cradle. Steel balls collide almost elastically. Equal masses swap velocities, so one ball swung in sends one ball out at the other end.
  • Where it stops working. The sim is head-on and one-dimensional. Real balls can glance off each other, spin, and touch for a finite time. The value of e is also not a fixed property of a material, and it can change with the speed of impact.
09

Summary

In one line. A collision's outcome is set by the masses, the velocities and the elasticity e, and the badges tally two totals so you can check it.

Key points

  • Σp is the same before and after every ball-to-ball collision.
  • KE is conserved only at e = 1. At e = 0 the balls stick and the KE loss is greatest.
  • A wall pushes from outside, so it can change Σp.

Common mix-ups

  • "An inelastic collision destroys momentum." It loses only kinetic energy. Σp is unchanged.
  • "Kinetic energy is conserved in every collision." It is conserved only when e = 1.
  • "The moving ball always stops dead in an elastic collision." It stops only when the masses are equal.

Things to try on your own

  • Choose any masses and velocities, work out Σp by hand, and compare it with the badge.
  • Set e = 0 and compare the KE lost with ½ [m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂)](v₁ − v₂)².
  • Turn the Reflecting border off, run the same collision, and compare how Σp behaves.
